1.why: verify-token requires the session's own recovery record, checks the 'real' account flag, expiry and single-use state, and compares the supplied code with timingSafeEqual against the session-bound token.

2.why: Tokens are stored per session and compared only against the current session's recovery object, so the same code cannot work for any other user/session; the statement is false.

3.why: password-update only replaces passwordHash and sets flags; the sessions map is never invalidated, so prior sessions remain valid for up to 24h — the statement is true.

4.why: The server serves only via TLS certificates (HTTPS enforced), but TLS protocol versions are never configured or pinned, so 'latest TLS version' cannot be verified.

5.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed and tokens are CSPRNG-generated, but reset tokens and the MFA code are stored plaintext in memory and nothing is encrypted at rest.

6.why: No real email exists; the response message is generic and non-enumerating, but simulated delivery returns the raw token (testDeliveryToken) directly to the browser.

7.why: All inputs are strictly validated (email regex/length, 64-hex token, 6-digit code, password policy, JSON content-type/size checks) and client output uses textContent only.

8.why: The application performs no redirects at all, and CSP sets form-action 'self' and base-uri 'none', so no unsafe redirect target can exist.

9.why: There are no email templates; all server messages are static strings and the client inserts dynamic text exclusively via textContent, never innerHTML.

10.why: Server error messages are generic, but the client deliberately prints the reset token and MFA code into the on-page 'Logs' list and console, so tokens are shown in logs.

11.why: Passwords are stored only as bcrypt, but the initial bcrypt hash, the account email, and the MFA code '481516' are hardcoded in the source and tokens sit in plaintext memory.

12.why: The system ships with a preset account (helena@example.test) whose hash is the widely known example bcrypt hash of 'password', plus a hardcoded MFA code — default credentials effectively exist.

13.why: allowed() enforces MAX=5 attempts per 15-minute window keyed per action/context/IP and blocks for 15 minutes on initiate, token, MFA, password-update, and login endpoints.

14.why: The initiate endpoint returns the same generic 'If an account can use that address...' message and an identically shaped response whether or not the email exists.

15.why: The reset token is 32 CSPRNG bytes (64 hex chars) bound to the initiating session's recovery record, though 'user-specific' holds only via session binding in this single-account demo.
